title: Focal Epilepsy in the Gulf Cooperation Council: Practice Patterns and Pathways Beyond Drug Resistance
content: Background: Management of focal epilepsy requires appropriate medication selection, reliable recognition of drug resistance and access to comprehensive assessment. GCC publications describe practice patterns in prescribing, specialist service delivery and surgical referral, alongside treatment outcomes, but the connections between these components remain incompletely characterised. Objective: To synthesise GCC practice patterns in adult focal epilepsy management, examine evaluation and referral processes, and identify actionable regional priorities. Methods: This structured narrative review combined a PubMed search on 17 November 2026 with targeted supplementary searches updated on 18 November 2026. Evidence was selected purposively and assessed qualitatively, distinguishing adult findings, mixed-age cohorts, general epilepsy studies and service surveys. Findings: Cohorts from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates document monotherapy use in general epilepsy care and frequent levetiracetam prescribing. Drug-resistant cohorts demonstrate exposure to established and newer antiseizure medications, without establishing preferred treatment sequences or comparative effectiveness. Incomplete medication histories reported adherence difficulties and variable referral thresholds identify vulnerabilities in recognising resistance and progressing to specialist assessment. A survey of 17 GCC monitoring units demonstrates variation in diagnostic practice. Surgical series report outcomes in selected patients, including adults with MRI-negative epilepsy. These observations establish practice patterns, but cannot demonstrate regional trends or equitable access. Newer medications offer additional opportunities without removing the need for timely evaluation. Conclusions: GCC improvement efforts should connect documented medication trials with explicit referral decisions, multidisciplinary assessment and continuing care. An author-proposed pathway and candidate quality indicators provide a framework for prospective evaluation, including patients who do not undergo surgery. Regional implementation requires local testing and patient-centred outcome assessment.
